To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the size of the effect of irrelevant speech on spoken word recognition in older and younger adults was the same.
the irrelevant speech effect is present in older adults and that older and younger adults do not show differential sensitivity to the irrelevant speech effect.
(1) older adults find it just as easy as younger adults to inhibit processing of irrelevant speech and (2) older adults find irrelevant noise just as distracting as younger adults.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how people use information from irrelevant sources to guide the interpretation of speech.
the question of whether the information content of irrelevant auditory sources has a differential effect on the spoken-word recognition of older and younger adults.
the role of the hippocampus in the acquisition of new information and its subsequent recall.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
older adults are not more susceptible to the cognitive-level effects of irrelevant speech.
older adults are able to inhibit the processing (cognitive level) of irrelevant speech, just like younger adults.

the information content of the masker is the critical variable in the irrelevant speech effect and that the effect of this information content on speech recognition does not differ for younger and older participants.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
older adults are no worse than younger adults at suppressing the processing of irrelevant information, at least in the context of spoken word recognition.
the effects of cognitive-level interference are similar for younger and older listeners.
the information content of irrelevant sources does not affect the processing of speech for older adults any differently than for younger adults.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the processing of speech is more complex and dynamic than previously thought, and that it is possible to separate the effects of different aspects of the auditory scene.
older adults are able to use their attentional control to reduce the interference from a cognitive-level source of irrelevant information.
older adults are able to use the same strategies as younger adults to overcome interference caused by the perception of irrelevant speech.
